Rijeka Jewish section on Kozala municipal cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Rijeka, Croatia

Rijeka, a major Adriatic seaport first mentioned in Roman times, developed into a significant industrial and naval center through the 19th century (49,806 residents by 1910). Jewish presence dates to 1436, though a formal community organized only in 1781; unusually heterogeneous compared to other Croatian Jewish communities, Rijeka's Jews came from Austria, Italy, Greece, Hungary, and Poland, with mid-19th-century Sephardic arrivals from Split and Dubrovnik following the 'minhag Ispalatto' rite. A first synagogue opened in 1832; two more followed in 1902 (small, Orthodox, serving Polish/Galician immigrants) and 1928 (large Neolog synagogue, designed in Art Nouveau style by architect Lipót Baumhorn). Population peaked at 2,000 by 1900. Though under relatively tolerant Italian rule before WWII, German occupation and Croatian annexation from 1943 brought severe repression - the large synagogue was burned in 1944, community archives destroyed, and 260 local Jews perished in the Holocaust. This cemetery site's history is complex: an 1840 first Jewish cemetery on private vineyard land drew local objections, leading the community to specified plots within the general Kozala cemetery from 1875, though actual operations didn't begin until 1904, when a three-room Ceremonial Hall (designed by Francesco Placsek) was inaugurated. Twenty-two tombstones from the original 1840 cemetery were incorporated into the current site's southern wall. The land was nationalized in 1976; a 1981 Holocaust memorial by architect Zdenko Sila names 278 local victims. A three-year renovation of the Ceremonial Hall was completed in 2021.
